with:
  for len(xs) >= 8 {
  		x := xs[:8:8]
  		// Carry-save reduction of 8 words into weighted bit-planes.
  		s1 := x[0] ^ x[1] ^ x[2]
  		c1 := (x[0] & x[1]) | (x[2] & (x[0] ^ x[1]))
  		s2 := x[3] ^ x[4] ^ x[5]
  		c2 := (x[3] & x[4]) | (x[5] & (x[3] ^ x[4]))
  		s3 := x[6] ^ x[7] ^ s1
  		c3 := (x[6] & x[7]) | (s1 & (x[6] ^ x[7]))
  		s := s2 ^ s3
  		c := s2 & s3
  		t := c1 ^ c2 ^ c3
  		d := (c1 & c2) | (c3 & (c1 ^ c2))
  		u := t ^ c
  		v := t & c
  		e := d ^ v
  		f := d & v
  		n += bits.OnesCount64(s) + 2*bits.OnesCount64(u) +
  			4*bits.OnesCount64(e) + 8*bits.OnesCount64(f)
  		xs = xs[8:]
  	}

responses:
## Analysis

The current program is a tail-handled, 8-way unrolled loop. Attempts 1–3 all produced the identical cost of 4622, which suggests the SSA optimizer already removes most of the bounds-check and slicing overhead. Changing indexing style alone won't help. Unrolling to 16 (Inspiration 2) scored worse, so the remaining cost is mostly the per-word `OnesCount64` work, not loop control.

The main lever left is to reduce the number of `OnesCount64` calls. A carry-save adder (Harley–Seal style) tree can compute the popcount of 8 words with 4 popcount calls plus about 26 bitwise ops, instead of 8 calls. That pays off if `OnesCount64` expands to a multi-instruction body in giri. If it is a single intrinsic instruction, this could be slightly worse, so this is a test rather than a guaranteed gain.

The weights work out as: total = pc(s) + 2·pc(u) + 4·pc(e) + 8·pc(f). I checked it by hand on an all-ones block (8 words, each column sums to 8), which gives 8 as expected. The tail logic stays the same, so correctness on the remainder cases is unchanged, and xs is never written.

## Expected effect

- Fewer `OnesCount64` calls per 8 words (4 instead of 8), which should reduce executed SSA instructions if the call is expensive in giri.
- The rest of the function (tail handling and return) is unchanged, so it stays correct on every length.
- If giri treats `OnesCount64` as cheap, this may score the same or slightly worse, and the result would tell us which regime we are in.
